item.title: 'High risk' of lake breaching and causing second flood, warns China
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckg8l2x8wr8o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'High risk' of lake breaching and causing second flood, warns China - Published China has warned there is a "high risk" that a lake which formed after the recent landslide near the Nepal-Tibet border may breach its banks, causing a second flood downstream. The warning comes after Wednesday's deadly flash flood in the same area which scientists say was triggered by the collapse of a mountain glacier into a river. As of Friday, an estimated 2.5 million cubic metres of water had accumulated at the barrier lake, according to state broadcaster CCTV. A barrier lake is a body of water formed when debris dams up a river. Officials said that three million cubic metres of water is expected to flow into the lake between Thursday and the weekend, posing a "high risk of breach". The area is also expected to see heavy rain in the coming days, according to state media. The barrier lake, which formed at the confluence of the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers, had started to overflow on Thursday, according to China's Ministry of Water Resources. Most of the Chinese emergency services had stopped at a village about 7km (4 mi) from Gyirong Port, the major land crossing linking Nepal and China which was hit by Wednesday's massive flood. This was because the barrier lake at that time was "overflowing non-stop" which could lead to fresh floods or debris flows, according to a CCTV report. But by Friday afternoon, state media reported that the "risk from the upstream barrier lake had come under control" and that rescue operations had resumed. Authorities have sent engineering teams to monitor the lake's water levels and the atmospheric conditions, and drones have been flown in to drop off equipment and supplies. - Tracing the deadly path of the Nepal-Tibet flash flood - Published16 hours ago - Collapsed glacier likely caused devastating Nepal-Tibet floods, scientists say - Published5 hours ago - What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods - Published1 hour ago The lake is near the Langtang Lirung peak, where the collapsed glacier is believed to have originated, and several kilometres upstream from Gyirong Port. Separately, Nepali authorities have warned of the risk of blockages causing further floods along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers. They have warned people to stay away from the rivers until further notice. Scientists have said that the flood on Wednesday was likely to have been caused by part of a glacier near Langtang Lirung collapsing into the river below, which in turn caused a massive surge downstream carrying water and debris. Several hundred people have died in Nepal and with hundreds more still missing after the flash flood. On the Tibet side of the border alone, more than 550 are missing - nearly half of which are foreigners.

item.title: Norway's King Harald dies aged 89
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clykn5p5172o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Norway's King Harald dies aged 89 - Published Norway's King Harald V has died at the age of 89, after he was taken to hospital last week for treatment for a rare blood condition. The palace in Oslo said he passed away peacefully at 06:35 local time (04:35GMT) on Friday at the national hospital in Oslo. The royal flag on the roof of the palace has been lowered to half-mast. In the 24 hours leading up to his death, members of the royal family had visited the king, and crowds had laid flowers at the palace. Harald was Norway's first king born in Norway since the 14th Century. He has been succeeded by his son Haakon, 53, who will hold an extraordinary council of state with the government later on Friday. King Charles III sent his "most heartfelt condolences", while King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden remembered "a good friend to me, my family and to Sweden", and wished his godson Haakon "success and good fortune". After 35 years on the throne, Harald will be remembered as a popular and reforming figure who modernised the monarchy, broke with tradition by marrying a commoner and served as a unifying figure at Norway's most difficult moments. Royal observers say he was down-to-earth, respected and beloved, describing him as a "grandfather" of the nation and the "People's king" - a title also used by his father King Olav V. In the wake of the 2011 bomb and gun attacks on Oslo and the island of Utøya, Harald appealed to Norwegians to support each other and not "let fear take over". More recently, Harald and his family faced health challenges and scandal, especially over his daughter-in-law Mette-Marit's association with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and her son Marius Borg Høiby's conviction for rape. During his reign, the Norwegian monarchy became more egalitarian and transparent with finances and health, Ole-Jørgen Schulsrud-Hansen, historian and TV2 royal correspondent, told the BBC. Tove Taalesen, royal correspondent for Nettavisen, described the late king as "one of us", while Caroline Vagle, royal expert for Se og Hør magazine, said he had "always been very close to the people". When Norway's national football team returned from the US after making it to the World Cup quarter-finals for the first time, Harald welcomed them home at the palace. He is survived by his wife of almost 58 years, Queen Sonja, their daughter Princess Märtha Louise, their son, the new King Haakon, and six grandchildren. Harald was born on 21 February 1937 on the Skaugum estate near Oslo, more than 30 years after Norway gained its independence from Sweden and became a constitutional monarchy. He was three when dictator Adolf Hitler ordered Norway's invasion by Nazi Germany early in World War Two. Harald's mother fled with her children across the border to Sweden, and they travelled to the US on the invitation of President Franklin D Roosevelt. Prince Harald returned with his family to Norway at the end of the war and completed his school and compulsory military service. He became crown prince in 1957, and studied social science, history and economics at Balliol College in Oxford from 1960 to 1962. He met Sonja Haraldsen, the daughter of a businessman, at a party, but the crown prince had to wait nine years before he was allowed to marry her. His father, King Olav, had always hoped he would marry a European princess. Eventually he told his father that if he could not marry Sonja, he would stay single, King Harald told Norway's public broadcaster, external. His father finally gave his consent, and the couple wed in Oslo Cathedral on 29 August 1968. Harald's choice paved the way for his own two children to marry commoners too, and for Vagle, that "helped bring an end to a very male-dominated Royal Family". "He has never been afraid to show emotion, humour or vulnerability, and that has made him very human," the royal expert said. When his father became ill in 1990, the crown prince became regent. Harald then ascended to the throne when Olav died on 17 January 1991. The new king came into his own around 2000, according to historian Trond Norén Isaksen, growing from a reserved, serious and shy man into someone who became much more open and empathetic. In July 2011 Harald faced his greatest challenge yet as king, when neo-Nazi Anders Breivik murdered eight people with a car bomb in Oslo before moving on to a youth camp on the island of Utøya, where he shot dead 69 others, most of them teenagers. He gave a televised address the next day, and weeks later he delivered a speech, empathising with the victims and their families as a father, grandfather, husband, and king. On the verge of tears, his voice quivered and broke. "I can only imagine the depth of your pain. As King of this nation, I feel for each and every one of you," he said. Looking back, historian Ole-Jørgen Schulsrud-Hansen said: "I think that moment has been burned into our minds of what a monarchy should be." In 2016, the king made headlines again by giving an impassioned speech , externalsupporting diversity of religion, ethnicity and sexual orientation. He said Norwegians are from "Afghanistan, Pakistan and Poland, from Sweden, Somalia, and Syria," they "believe in God, Allah, the Universe and nothing", and they "are girls who love girls, boys who love boys, and girls and boys who love each other". The king was also a keen athlete and environmentalist - one of the initiators of the Norwegian branch of the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), who served as president of the Norwegian chapter for 20 years. He was such an accomplished sailor, he represented Norway three times at the Olympics, and declared his competitive sailing days over in 2022. When Crown Prince Haakon married Mette-Marit in 2001, the king and queen welcomed her four-year-old son from a previous relationship. Marius Borg Høiby was treated as one of the family, but the royal house later stressed he was never a royal. The king's daughter Princess Märtha Louise initially married a Norwegian writer before controversially remarrying in 2024 to an American self-styled shaman. The couple's business activities eventually led to her halting her royal duties. While some Norwegians may have felt Harald was too lenient with his family's controversial life decisions, Vagle believes he had "shown himself to be someone who puts talking things through ahead of issuing harsh instructions". As the king's health declined, he permanently reduced his public engagements in April 2024. More recently he was treated with cortisone for a rare blood condition, haemolytic anaemia, which causes the number of red blood cells in the body to be reduced. He entered hospital on 17 August and his son became regent, taking over his activities. This year alone the Norwegian royal family has faced compounded personal health challenges and scandals that have left them under almost constant public scrutiny. The rape trial of Marius Borg Høiby, convicted of a litany of offences by judges in Oslo in June, hung over the royal family for many months. He has now appealed against a four-year jail term and appeared at Harald's bedside shortly before he died. Days before the trial began, documents were released revealing his mother Mette-Marit's frequent contact with late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. She later apologised to King Harald and Queen Sonja for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement", adding in a national TV interview that she wished she had never met him. Two days after her son's trial came to an end, Mette-Marit received a lung transplant. She had been diagnosed with a rare form of pulmonary fibrosis eight years earlier. Her doctors will not declare her stable until a year after the transplant, and King Haakon will face a difficult period of succession as he continues to support her. The crises surrounding the monarchy have had an effect on its popularity. One poll for Aftenposten newspaper found that support had dropped from 72% in 2024 to 54%. Other polls suggested almost half of Norwegians believed Mette-Marit could no longer become queen, although Haakon is now highly likely to say she will become queen. Despite that negative sentiment towards the monarchy, Vagle said criticism was rarely directed at the late king personally, leaving her with the impression that "everyone has loved King Harald". "When things go wrong in the royal family, people tend to blame anyone but the king," historian Trond Norén Isaksen remarked. Haakon has faced questions about how the turbulence surrounding his own household will "follow him into his position as a king", according to Tove Taalesen, however she believes he has shown leadership and dealt with recent events well. The royal family's main strategy has been to separate itself from Marius Borg Høiby's trial, and Ole-Jørgen Schulsrud-Hansen believes that has largely succeeded. Although there may be further scrutiny over the Epstein files, the focus for Norwegians now will be on remembering a "greatly beloved king" and supporting his son.

item.title: Trump administration illegally retaliated against Anthropic, judge rules
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2q7z5mlrmo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Trump administration illegally retaliated against Anthropic, judge rules - Published A judge has ruled the US Department of Defense acted unlawfully when it designated artificial intelligence (AI) startup Anthropic a supply chain risk, calling the move "illegal and baseless". The company argued in the lawsuit that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth overstepped his authority with the new designation. It followed Anthropic's refusal to allow the military to use its AI models for things that included surveillance or autonomous weapons. US district judge Rita Lin said in the ruling that citing national security "is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics". Anthropic welcomed the ruling. The BBC has contacted the Pentagon and the White House for comment. Anthropic is focused on "working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology," a spokesperson told the BBC. Judge Lin said in the court filing that the Defense Department had acted unlawfully to order firms that do business with the US military to boycott Anthropic. The Pentagon designated Anthropic as a supply-chain risk in February - a law typically reserved for companies based in countries that pose a threat to the US. It marked the first time an American company had been publicly designated as such. Anthropic's lawsuit said the government's actions were both "unprecedented and unlawful". The Claude-maker said its models were not reliable enough to be safely used in weapons systems for the military. It added that it opposed its use for domestic surveillance as a violation of rights. The Pentagon said at the time that private companies should not be able to constrain military action. The White House had previously said Anthropic was "a radical left, woke company" attempting to control military activity" and argued the military was beholden to the US Constitution, "not any woke AI company's terms of service". The Pentagon also argued that Anthropic's refusal to accept new contract terms raised concerns over what the company could do with its technology. Anthropic said in its lawsuit that its business had been impacted by the government's actions and its right to freedom of speech had been violated. Judge Lin said during an earlier round in the lawsuit that the government was trying to "cripple" the company and "chill public debate" over military use of AI. "This appears to be classic First Amendment retaliation," the judge added. - Published1 day ago - Published9 June

item.title: Tate brothers blast US jail conditions as they seek bail in UK extradition fight
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9v9nndjznvo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Tate brothers blast US jail conditions as they seek bail in UK extradition fight - Published Andrew and Tristan Tate have told a Florida court they should be released from jail so they can fight extradition to the UK on charges of rape and trafficking. Wearing tan jail uniforms, the brothers maintained they did not commit the alleged crimes as they hit out at conditions in US custody. Government lawyers argued that the two were a flight risk and had bragged about having multiple passports, while defence attorneys said the two social media influencers' high profile would make it almost impossible for them to flee. US Magistrate Judge Lauren Louis will issue a written ruling at a later date on whether to grant bail to the dual British-US citizens. The two were arrested in Miami on 19 July. During Thursday's hearing, defence lawyers said the pair had complied with the terms of their release while they battled the UK charges and another case in Romania. US authorities took the men into custody last month after the UK's Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) unveiled dozens of new charges against them. The British authorities have until 16 September to submit a full extradition request. - Will the Tate brothers be extradited from the US to the UK? - Published21 July The brothers, who arrived in court in shackles, were questioned in turn by their defence attorneys and government lawyers as they took the stand. Andrew Tate, 39, declared he has "never committed the crimes I'm accused of". Tristan Tate, 38, described his detention conditions as small and hot, with little sunlight and exercise. "It's beginning to grate on me because I can't partake in helping with my defence," he told the court, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner. "It's death by scurvy," he said, adding that he had lost 14lb (6.3kg). The British Embassy filed court documents asking the judge to keep the Tates in custody as the UK pursues extradition. US government lawyers pushed back against the brothers' claims that they had exaggerated their wealth to massage their online personas. The federal attorneys said the Tates had access to resources that could help fund an escape and they had bragged about having multiple passports. But Andrew Tate, a former professional kickboxer, testified that to support himself financially, he "had to go back to the boxing ring against heavier, younger opponents", according to CBS News. "I've said some stupid things, but sometimes you have to shake the internet to get noticed," he testified about his online statements, according to CBS. "This is the reality of the internet. "I'm being treated like El Chapo," he added, referring to the Mexican drug kingpin, "but I have a perfect record in the court system". Under questioning from his attorney, Joseph McBride, Andrew Tate denied he was a human trafficker. The defence also called Natasha Sesay, from England, to testify in support of releasing Andrew Tate. She described a five-year romantic relationship, saying she had had one child with him and was expecting a second. "It's nice having him at home," she told the court, reports CBS. Sesay also said that despite his online persona, Andrew Tate "has never ever been violent toward women", according to CBS. The UK has brought a total of 59 criminal charges against the Tates, including rape and counts relating to sex trafficking and indecent images of a child. The British authorities filed 21 charges last year against the brothers, then 38 additional counts last month. The combined charges involve seven accusers, UK prosecutors said. The brothers also faced sex-trafficking charges in Romania in 2022, and were under a travel ban until they were allowed to come to the US in 2025. "If I go to England they will lock me up," Tristan Tate said on the stand in Miami on Thursday, "and take everything I've ever worked for". He also said the Romanian charges had "destroyed my entire life", reports CBS. "They took everything, even the savings accounts for their [his children's] college funds. This case is make or break for me." The Tates built an influencer empire in the so-called manosphere, showcasing a lifestyle of conspicuous wealth and excess. Andrew Tate accumulated millions of followers among an audience of primarily young men. The White House has said President Donald Trump will not intervene in the extradition case of the brothers, who have been vocal supporters of him. item.title: What we know after the big Grand Theft Auto 6 preview
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3d7exngd5no?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
What we know after the big Grand Theft Auto 6 preview - Published After more than 18 months since the last official glimpse of Grand Theft Auto 6, developer Rockstar has shown fans a 26-minute preview of the upcoming blockbuster video game. Its "extended look" debuted on Netflix, six hours before going live on YouTube, and was the first chance players have had to see detailed footage of the title in action. The montage, with no commentary or explanatory captions, showed off improved graphics, detailed environments and a selection of car-chases and shoot-outs from the sequel. The broadcast followed a week of unauthorised gameplay leaks, which the developer said it had been "heartbreaking" to see shared online. After it got its chance to show the version of GTA 6 it wanted the world to see, here are some things we learned, and some things we still don't know. Two's company The extended look spent a long time showcasing the relationship between protagonists Jason Duval and Lucia Camino, the couple at the centre of GTA 6's "Bonnie and Clyde" story. In a preview published on website IGN, external, the developers said the characters' story - and the way it unfolds - can be affected by the player's actions, although they can "opt out" of developing the pair's bond if they want. The Netflix preview didn't show this playing out in detail, but did show the ability to change control between the two characters at different points. In one segment, Jason was seen lowering Lucia from a window as they escaped from a drug bust in a block of apartments. A similar switching system was used in Grand Theft Auto 5, which had three playable main characters. 'The best-looking game' Praise for GTA 6's graphics was more or less universal, with characters displaying photorealistic faces and lifelike movements. Fans were also impressed by the detailed locations on show, which included the interiors of apartments, rooftop bars and sleazy underground clubs. The preview also showcased the various environments of Leonida, the fictional, Florida-inspired US state where GTA 6 is set. The range of different body shapes and sizes among background characters - something rarely seen in video games - was also highlighted by many players watching online. Journalist Ryan McCaffrey said GTA 6 "might be the best-looking game I've ever seen". The impressive visual fidelity has been attributed to the amount of time Rockstar has spent working on the game, and its budget, which is thought to be among the most expensive in video game history. It's still Grand Theft Auto While GTA 6 appears to break new ground in terms of visuals and scale, it is still, at its heart, a Grand Theft Auto game. During the preview, viewers saw the armed heists, car chases and criminal underworld scenes that have become a trademark of the series. Satirical swipes at US culture, darkly comic interactions between characters and a huge range of optional side activities were all present once again. And Rockstar appears to have expanded on features it introduced in its last major release, 2018 hit Red Dead Redemption 2, such as an "honour" system that affects the player's reputation among other characters. Fans of the series, which is estimated to have sold half a billion copies since it launched in 1997, will have been thrilled to see it. No news on GTA 6 Online Rockstar had already stated that GTA 6 will be a "single-player experience" on launch, leaving fans to assume a follow-up to the incredibly successful online element of its previous games would come later. The Netflix preview was dedicated to showing off the story and gameplay, and was not necessarily expected to highlight any new multiplayer features. Although the launch of the game on 19 November is widely expected to be the biggest of all time, the long-term success of GTA 6 will be judged on how well Rockstar converts players to any new online mode. GTA online, which also launched after the release of GTA 5, remains one of the most-played games in the world, and is thought to have generated billions of dollars for Rockstar. The previous game in the series, GTA 5, also broke records when it came out in 2013 and has sold more than 200 million copies since. Two official trailers for the sixth game have almost 500 million combined views on YouTube, and the Netflix "extended look" on Thursday is being marketed as an event by the streaming service. Next month the company is due to appear at an employment tribunal in Scotland to defend itself against claims it illegally sacked a group of ex-employees for trying to form a union. It strongly denies the accusations, and says the workers were fired on the grounds of gross misconduct. Additional reporting by Thomas Fabbri. item.title: Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgwdn1g58yo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America - Published US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order seeking to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America. The move comes after trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed last week, and the US imposed new 50% tariffs on $20bn (C$28bn) worth of Canadian goods. Canada will implement "dollar for dollar" counter tariffs next month. Trump said the move to rename the lake, which straddles both countries, was effective immediately. He has broad discretion over how the US recognises landmarks but other countries do not have to follow. In response, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said "things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario - today and forever". Text of the executive order says it gives the US Department of the Interior 30 days to update the name change with the Geographic Names Information Service - the official repository of domestic geographic names in the US. Carney noted that the name Lake Ontario could be traced back more than 400 years, adding that it preceded the formation of the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence. "We know that the United States is changing. Their trade relations, their foreign policy, their national monuments, their hydronyms. "Canadian women and men also know that things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario - today and forever." There is no universally recognised international body setting the names of international waters. When Trump took to the White House in 2025, he signed a similar order that changed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water. It also led to a legal dispute between Mexico and tech giant Google, which renamed the gulf in its maps application., external In that case, Google Maps users in the US see "Gulf of America", while those in Mexico see the "Gulf of Mexico". Those in other countries see the "Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America)". The White House at the time also blocked Associated Press reporters from presidential events over the news agency's refusal to adopt the name "Gulf of America" in its coverage. The AP sued the Trump administration in response, and that legal battle is ongoing. Canadian officials dismissed Trump's move to rename the lake. Ontario Premier Doug Ford wrote: "It's Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever." Other premiers and ministers made similar statements. The names of four of the Great Lakes - Ontario, Huron, Michigan and Erie - originate from indigenous words. Lake Superior was named after an anglicised French word. Lake Ontario, the smallest of the Great Lakes, borders both the Canadian province and the US state of New York. There was a mixed reaction from US politicians. Trump's Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum applauded the move, writing: "We're on it, Mr. President!" "The places and waters that border our nation and support our economy should reflect the greatness of the United States," he said, adding that the US Geological Survey "maps our country for the world to see, and we are PROUD to implement your Executive Order to rename LAKE AMERICA". But Democratic lawmaker Debbie Dingell of Michigan, the US state that borders four of the five Great Lakes, said that she would introduce a bill in Congress to nullify the name change, calling Trump's order "idiotic". She wrote: "The Great Lakes are a shared treasure that generations of Americans and Canadians have worked together to protect". Democratic New York Governor Kathy Hochul said her state, the sole US state bordering Lake Ontario, would not be calling it Lake America. As he signed the order on Thursday in the Oval Office, Trump said it was not a direct message to Canada, but that America's northern neighbour "has been ripping us off for a long time on trade". US-Canada relations have fallen to new lows, with insults thrown back and forth over the past week. But there was a hint on Thursday that there was room for a return to the negotiating table. Canadian US trade minister, Dominic LeBlanc, said the US had withdrawn some of its demands around labelling requirements in French, one of the sticking points. The US has maintained it never made demands about language. Both sides have accused the other of demanding last-minute changes that caused the breakdown in trade negotiations. - Canada's retaliation tests the limit of American power under Trump - Published2 days ago - 'Half my business will be gone' - firms in Canada and US fear trade war - Published3 days ago Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's weekly US Politics Unspun newsletter. item.title: Selena Gomez pushes back against 'frivolous' fraud claims
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cz0z4k28804o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Selena Gomez pushes back against 'frivolous' fraud claims - Published Selena Gomez's social media accounts brim with adoring fans: two million likes for her most recent post showing her and her husband in a rose-petal strewn hotel, and thousands of comments praising her beauty, her lipstick and the perfume brand she founded. This week the PR focus for the star – who rose to fame on the Disney channel but has moved into song-writing, films and TV drama – was supposed to be on the upcoming series six of Only Murders in the Building that sees its podcasting sleuths transfered to London for their next adventure. But the wider chat, outside those friendly spaces, has gone off-script and is largely on a less flattering topic, namely claims from investors who allege she breached her contract by not properly backing the mental health platform Wondermind that she cofounded with her mother five years ago. As a result, the five investors argue, they were defrauded of the nearly $1.2m they invested. Gomez is pushing back against those allegations - her lawyer has asked that she be dismissed from the case altogether, saying the claims made against her are "threadbare" and arguing she should never have been "dragged into" the case at all. The investors claim they were told that "Selena Gomez, one of the most famous women on earth, with a billion-dollar brand and a platform unmatched in social media, would be actively building the company as its head of marketing". Gomez's attorney Matthew Rosengart says their allegations are "vague, generalised and contradictory" and that Gomez never agreed to, and did not, manage the company, or make the kind of commitments they are suggesting. "The claims against her are meritless if not frivolous," he said. Mr Rosengart added that the legal team was "exploring other avenues of relief for Ms. Gomez including sanctions against plaintiffs". The emphatic pushback from Gomez may reflect a concern for her reputation but it also leaves her mother in the hot-seat, facing the fraud allegations alongside the company itself and a third co-founder. Crisis PR commentator, Lauren Beeching, founder of Honest London says Gomez is far from the first celebrity to try working with a close family member. At times it can come off like in the Jenner-Kardashian household or with the tennis-playing Williams sisters. But there are plenty of examples - from the Beckhams' to Britney Spears - where family brands and business don't mix well. Working with close relatives, whether that's a sibling or a parent, or someone else is almost always a higher risk approach, says Beeching. "It can make the boundaries between the personal relationship with the business and the celebrity's reputation much harder to separate," she says. The natural level of trust means that you might not apply the same rules as you would in a normal commercial relationhsip, so better guardrails are needed, she says. "If you're going into business [as a] family, I'd put more structure around it, not less, for sure. "Define everybody's responsibilities, bring in independent oversight, and decide what happens if something goes wrong before something goes wrong." "A family relationship shouldn't be a company's governance structure." At the end of the day Gomez may not need to worry too much over this case, says Beeching. "This will generate headlines because Selena Gomez is enormously famous, but I don't think it's the type of story her core audience is particularly interested in," she says. "There's an important difference between generating negative headlines and causing lasting reputational damage. " Still, for celebrities considering trading on their personal brand, Beeching does have words of advice. "Before lending your name to a company, don't ask what your reputation could do for the business. Ask what that business can eventually do for your reputation as well." item.title: Optimus Prime and Eeyore voice actor Peter Cullen dies
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c15844gwe0wo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Optimus Prime and Eeyore voice actor Peter Cullen dies - Published Actor Peter Cullen, who voiced popular characters including Optimus Prime in Transformers and Eeyore in Disney's Winnie the Pooh franchise, has died at the age of 85. The Canadian actor began his most famous role - as the heroic deep-voiced Optimus Prime - for the Transformers TV series in 1984, then returned for seven Hollywood films from 2007 to 2023 and other spin-offs. He voiced depressive donkey Eeyore in TV animation The New Adventures of Winnie the Pooh from the late 1980s as well as numerous related shows, films and games. His other memorable voice parts included KARR, the evil counterpart to KITT in TV show Knight Rider; the clicking vocalisations of The Predator in Arnold Schwarzenegger's 1987 film; and the roars of King Kong in 1976. He died on Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles, a statement said. "Peter Cullen passed away peacefully, surrounded by his loving family - and held in the hearts of his many friends and countless fans worldwide. "His family asks that you honour his remarkable legacy by serving your communities and leading others with compassion, integrity, and loyalty and always remember 'be strong enough to be gentle'." Cullen started his career on Canadian TV and radio and was then a regular on programmes like The Sonny & Cher Show before deciding to concentrate on voice acting. Brother's advice His Optimus Prime voice was inspired by his older brother, a decorated US Marine and Vietnam War veteran, who suggested he should play the character as "a real hero, don't be a Hollywood hero". "He said, 'Don't go yelling and screaming. He's strong enough to be gentle.' "And that resonated with me, and I could hear his voice all the way to the audition. When he drops down, when he gets serious, is where I found Optimus Prime." Cullen gave his brother a cut of the wages he received for playing Optimus Prime until his death. The actor's performance as the character earned him a Daytime Emmy nomination for outstanding performer in an animated programme in 2011, and he was honoured with a lifetime achievement award at the Children's & Family Emmy Awards in 2023. Cullen's other roles included Monterey Jack in Chip 'n Dale Rescue Rangers, and he voiced characters in 1980s and 90s animated series including Spider-Man, Donkey Kong, Alvin & the Chipmunks, Dungeons & Dragons, My Little Pony, Duck Tales and Gummi Bears.

item.title: Jury deliberating in trial of Lindsay Clancy, US woman accused of killing her children
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c33keeyyv70o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Jury deliberating in trial of Lindsay Clancy, US woman accused of killing her children - Published Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide The fate of US mother Lindsay Clancy is now in the hands of a Massachusetts jury, who must decide if she is guilty of first-degree murder - the intentional and premeditated killing of another person - in the deaths of her three children. For five weeks, the trial has gripped the country as Clancy's lawyers have argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis when she killed her children, who ranged in age from eight months to five years. Clancy does not deny killing her two sons and daughter. The prosecution argued she made a calculated decision to intentionally murder them. The jury could find Clancy guilty of first-degree murder, guilty of lesser charges, or not guilty. The jury of nine women and three men completed their first day of deliberations on Thursday. They will return on Friday. In the state of Massachusetts, a first-degree murder conviction carries a mandatory life in prison sentence without the possibility of parole. The jury could instead find Clancy guilty of second-degree murder - committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning - or involuntary manslaughter - causing death because of extreme carelessness. Those convictions, too, would lead to some prison time. If Clancy is found not guilty by reason of insanity, then she will not be set free, but instead sent to a psychiatric hospital, where she possibly could remain for life. Attorneys for both sides made closing arguments on Thursday before the jury began deliberating. Kevin Reddington, Clancy's lawyer, repeated the defence's argument that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis when she killed the children with exercise bands at their home and then attempted to end her own life by jumping out of a window. Clancy was paralysed by the attempt and has attended the trial in a wheelchair. "This young lady is not guilty of the killing of her children because she was suffering from a disease and defect," Reddington said, adding that he believed prosecutors were "not going to be able to prove otherwise". The UK's National Health Service (NHS) defines postpartum psychosis as a rare and serious mental health illness that can affect someone soon after having a baby, and which should be treated as a medical emergency. One of the more tense moments of the closing arguments came when Reddington directly addressed the prosecutors and asked them to explain why they tried to prove Clancy's suicide attempt was not serious. The judge interrupted and ordered him to address only the jury. Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague did not dispute that Clancy was mentally ill, but told the jury that the defendant could tell the difference between right and wrong at the time of the killings. "It's not the system or the DSM that caused her to strangle her kids," Sprague told the jury, referencing the US encyclopaedia of mental heath diagnoses, which does not give postpartum psychosis its own classification. Sprague also said Clancy had an "abundance of care", but had hidden thoughts from doctors about harming her kids. If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide. www.befrienders.org. In the UK a list of organisations that can help is available at bbc.co.uk/actionline. - Published19 August

item.title: Two killed in 'domestic violence incident' at school near Berlin
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgqdy8g2zlgo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Two killed in 'domestic violence incident' at school near Berlin - Published Two people have been killed in a "domestic violence incident" at a school in the town of Gosen-Neu Zittau near the German capital Berlin, local police have said. Brandenburg state police said they arrested a 19-year-old German man, who is "considered a prime suspect". They said it was not a "mass shooting", without specifying what weapon was used. It is not yet known if the suspect was a student at the private Docemus school. One of the dead was an 18-year-old secondary school female student and the other victim was a 30-year-old man who died when he tried to intervene, local media reported. The arrested suspect is believed to be the ex-boyfriend of the 18-year-old victim, Maz Online reported. Ulrike Liedtke, the speaker of Brandenburg's regional parliament, called the incident a "cowardly femicide". "The fact that we once again had to witness deadly violence against a woman fills me with deep sorrow and anger. "I am shaken that a citizen who showed moral courage and wanted to help also lost his life in this terrible act," Liedtke said. State premier Dietmar Woidke said it was an "unimaginable act of violence". The school's managing director Michael Kunz said classes will be cancelled on Friday. Although there would be no regular classes, Kunz said the school would remain open for all students who wished to come. "We want to provide them with a safe space where they can come together, talk to each other, and process what has happened," he said. A "very careful" decision will be made in coming days about how school life will be structured, he added. Last month in a separate attack, two girls were seriously wounded and a 16-year-old suspect arrested at a secondary school in southern Germany. - Published6 days ago

item.title: Man who attacked nun on CCTV in Jerusalem acquitted on grounds of mental health
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cpwl54kddeko?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Man who attacked nun on CCTV in Jerusalem acquitted on grounds of mental health - Published An Israeli court has acquitted a Jewish man who attacked a nun in Jerusalem, in an incident caught on CCTV which drew widespread condemnation. Jerusalem Magistrates Court said Yona Schreiber was experiencing a psychotic episode when he pushed over and kicked the French nun in the Old City in occupied East Jerusalem in April. It ruled that he was not criminally responsible for his actions and ordered him to be sent to a psychiatric hospital for up to six years. Video of the attack caused outrage, and deepened concerns after a rise in harassment of Christian clergy and pilgrims by Jewish extremists in the Old City. The victim, who hit her head on a stone block, suffered a bruised face and leg. Schreiber, 36, had been charged with assault motivated by hostility towards a religious group. According to the district psychiatrist's report, Schreiber "was in a psychotic state at the time of the act and is not substantively fit to stand trial". The prosecution accepted the psychiatrist's opinion and asked for Schreiber to be acquitted and committed to hospital. Judge Ofir Tishler said that although Schrieber had attacked the nun, he was ordering his acquittal due to his mental health. At the time of the attack, the French Consulate in Jerusalem said it strongly condemned Schreiber's "aggression". The director of the French Biblical and Archaeological School, where the nun is a researcher, called the assault an "act of sectarian violence". Israel's foreign ministry denounced the attack, calling it a "shameful act [which] stands in direct contradiction to the values of respect, coexistence, and religious freedom upon which Israel is founded and to which it remains deeply committed." "Israel remains firmly committed to safeguarding freedom of religion and freedom of worship for all faiths, and to ensuring that Jerusalem remains a city where every community can live, pray, and practice its faith in safety and dignity," the ministry said on X. While the violence of the attack on the nun is unusual, in the past few years in Jerusalem's Old City there have been regular cases of religious Jews spitting and acting aggressively towards those wearing Christian religious dress or symbols. Church properties have been vandalised and there have also been bitter disputes caused by settler takeovers. Church leaders accuse Israel of trying to change the status quo – long-standing agreements on ownership and responsibilities - at their holy places. A 2025 report by the Rossing Center, a Jerusalem-based organisation which aims to foster better inter-faith relations in the Holy Land, describes a "recent surge in overt animosity towards Christianity", putting this down to "a continued deepening of polarisation and ultra-nationalist political trends".

item.title: Board of Peace's Gaza envoy criticises Israeli strikes and Hamas actions
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cew92l07kwzo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Board of Peace's Gaza envoy criticises Israeli strikes and Hamas actions - Published A senior official on US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has criticised Israel's continuing air strikes on Gaza, as well as the actions of the Palestinian armed group Hamas. Nickolay Mladenov warned that a collapse of last October's ceasefire would be "a point of no return" for the region. He was speaking to the UN Security Council after Israel rejected the 15-point roadmap for Hamas's disarmament, which was announced by the Board of Peace last month. Hamas has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal. But Israel has insisted that the group must fully disarm before any pullout. At least 1,303 Palestinians, including 300 children, have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the US-brokered ceasefire began, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The Israeli military says four of its soldiers have been killed in Palestinian attacks in Gaza over the same period. The Board of Peace's high representative for Gaza told the Security Council on Wednesday that he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had agreed at their last meeting on a mechanism through which his government's remaining questions would be settled and that committees had been established for that purpose. Mladenov said that process had not stalled but warned that risks remained, including the continued killing of Palestinian civilians in Israeli strikes. "A ceasefire in fact under which civilians are still buried is not yet one that the people of Gaza can really feel. Every use of force that does not answer an immediate threat, and every incident that the deconfliction mechanism was not asked to resolve, costs this process something very hard to buy back," he added. Mladenov acknowledged that Hamas too had yet to meet fully its commitment to cease all military activities. "Every weapon carried, every tunnel still worked and every convoy still obstructed sets the process back and hands an argument to those who want to resume war," he said. He repeated that under the new roadmap, Israeli troop withdrawal from Gaza "follows verified decommissioning" of Hamas weapons handed over to the Palestinian technocratic committee that will govern Gaza under the Board of Peace's supervision. "It is sequenced and reciprocal," he said. That is a key difference from comments made by President Trump's envoy, Jared Kushner, after meeting Israel's prime minister two weeks ago. He said Israeli withdrawal would be discussed only once the demilitarisation of Gaza was "done" - appearing to change the plan in line with Israel's demands. Israel's representative told the Security Council meeting that it was committed to last October's US-brokered plan for ending the Gaza war, but she insisted it could not succeed while Hamas still had weapons, tunnels and other military infrastructure. "Disarmament must come first," she stated. The Palestinian representative said Israel was killing Palestinian civilians with impunity in Gaza and called on the international community to protect them without delay. Mladenov warned that if the ceasefire was allowed to collapse, "there will be no roadmap to return to, there will be no administration to deploy, and there will be nothing left of the ground to rebuild". "That would not be a setback. It would be a point of no return for everyone." The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage. Israel responded by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 73,430 people have been killed, according to the territory's health ministry.

item.title: Thieves steal Bronze Age artefacts from Spanish museum in four-minute heist
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgw9gw34yqo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Thieves steal Bronze Age artefacts from Spanish museum in four-minute heist - Published Thieves have stolen jewellery and artefacts from one of the most important prehistoric gold collections at a museum in the Spanish province of Alicante. The Treasure of Villena is a unique trove of almost ten kilos of gold, bowls, bottles and bracelets dating back to the Bronze Age. Police are still assessing exactly how many items were stolen in the raid, which took place in the early hours of Thursday morning. The museum confirmed to the BBC that rings, bowls and bracelets were among the items seized. It is the latest high profile heist on a European museum. Last year, thieves staged a brazen robbery at the Louvre in Paris in broad daylight. The operation at Villena Museum was "super fast and super professional", a spokesman for Villena town council said. The city council said the robbery began with a diversion. Around 05:15 local time (03:15 GMT), the alarms went off at the local sports centre, sending police there first, Spanish media reported. The museum's alarm then went off around 05:20. It took the thieves just four minutes to sweep through museum and leave the building before officers arrived. The Mayor of Villena, Fulgencio Cerdán, said the thieves "stole a large part of the treasure," specifically all the gold, El Pais reported. The museum's collection, which dates back to around 1,000 BC, is mainly gold items, but there are also pieces of silver, iron and amber. It consists of more than 60 bronze age objects, including 29 bracelets, 11 bowls, three bottles and other miscellaneous pieces. The town is "devastated," Cerdán said. "They've taken most of the treasure." "I'm even trembling. The truth is that for those of us from Villena, this destroys us. It's part of our heritage, of our wealth," the mayor said. The collection was discovered in 1963 by archaeologist Jose María Soler in a vessel sunk in a dried-out riverbed in Villena. The Villena council spokesman insisted there had been "no failure" by the museum. "All security systems were activated." The past year has seen a series of raids on European museums. In October 2025, thieves broke into the Louvre museum in Paris in broad daylight, stealing jewellery worth $102m (£75m) before escaping on scooters, in a heist that took about eight minutes. Last week, four works "of extraordinary value" by Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum in Sicily, Italy's culture ministry said. Earlier this month, Italian police said they had recovered paintings by Renoir, Cezanne and Matisse worth over $10.4m (£7.6m) which were stolen from the Magnani-Rocca Foundation museum near Parma. item.title: Jellyfish force partial shutdown of French nuclear plant
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy8znx3g4e2o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Jellyfish force partial shutdown of French nuclear plant - Published A massive influx of jellyfish has led to the partial shutdown of a nuclear reactor in northern France. Two of Gravelines nuclear power station's six units were shut down on Wednesday and Thursday because of the presence of jellyfish in the seawater filtration system, which is used for cooling, Électricité de France (EDF) said. A third unit has been shut down since 10 August due to the same issue, while a fourth has been closed for an inspection. Gravelines, one of the country's biggest nuclear power stations located between Dunkirk and Calais in the Hauts-de-France region, was also closed last August because of jellyfish in its filters. EDF said that units three, four and six were now shut. Unit three had only been reconnected to the grid on 18 August after the first wave of jellyfish earlier this month, the company said, while units one and two were also operating at reduced power as a preventative measure. Gravelines' six units each produce 900 megawatts of power. The station is cooled from a canal connected to the North Sea. Several species of jellyfish are native and can be seen around the coast when the waters are warm. Jellyfish are at their most active in the warmer months. Hot weather increases plankton levels at the water's surface, drawing jellyfish up, experts say. Measures have been implemented to try to prevent jellyfish infiltration, including a partnership with fishermen who capture and release them further offshore, according to French outlet Ici. There have been similar issues at other nuclear stations, including at the Torness plant in Scotland in 2011 and Sweden's Oskarshamn plant in 2013, but such cases are rare. item.title: 'The flood took everything': Nepal survivors describe horror of loved ones being swept away
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd08z840p8lo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'The flood took everything': Nepal survivors describe horror of loved ones being swept away - Published Survivors of massive flash floods in Nepal have recounted how they saw their loved ones disappear into torrents of mud. At least 469 people have died and several hundred others are missing after floods wiped out entire villages on the border of Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, with a force so powerful seismologists initially identified it as an earthquake. Rescuers trudged through thick mud and debris on Thursday as Nepalese authorities rushed to bring aid and relief supplies to the affected areas. "My family members were swept away by the flood in front of my eyes," Kalpana Malla from Nepal's Nuwakot district told the BBC. Malla said her father, mother, sister and sister's children were all claimed by the disaster. "They could not escape the flood; there was no chance at all," she said. "This flood took everything, but my son and I climbed the rooftop of a house and survived but couldn't explain how." Her son, Sugam Malla, said he saved his mother by pulling her hand. He said he had given his phone to his sister so she could keep in touch, but the mobile was no longer reachable. "I am worried she must be swept away." Another woman, Goma Pandit, said she had lost her buffaloes and all her other cattle. "My farmland is also swept away. Ten sacks of mustard seeds, tons of corn and rice paddy are all gone. Nothing is left." At Kathmandu's TU Teaching Hospital, families of those missing in the floods wait anxiously for updates. Holding up her phone, Ram Khumari Shrestha says: "This is my husband. He was off to Rasuwa as a part of his driving job. He was in contact with me until 8 pm yesterday. "But I couldn't call him this morning. The phone was switched off," she told the BBC. Mani Shrestha Bishwa was also camped out at the hospital on Wednesday night, hoping to hear from his younger brother, cousin, uncle and friend. "I last contacted them at 8:30 in the morning," he said. Trekking guide Sonam Dorjee missed the flood in his home village of Rasiwa Syafru by about an hour. He had left at 08:00 local time. As he was driving to Kathmandu, Dorjee told the BBC he had heard the sound of floods gushing into their village. "It [sounded] like an earthquake," he said. "My house has collapsed... I have seen a photo." Dorjee said his sister, Dechen Tamang, was missing, along with her husband and several other family members. He described the flood as "sudden and devastating". "Many survivors are now left without homes and they need emergency rescue and evacuation, as well as food, temporary accommodation and medical support." He is praying his sister is found alive. "There is a 10% chance, we hope," he said. Related topics - Published1 hour ago

item.title: What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd948kn02e5o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods - Published Massive landslides and flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have caused widespread damage and left hundreds dead or missing. Search and rescue operations have been ongoing since Wednesday's disaster. Chinese state media has said there are significant casualties, while Nepalese officials describe "huge scale loss". But rescuers are on edge because of the risk of further flooding. A lake of rising water which has formed at a site along the border briefly overflowed early on Friday, prompting Chinese authorities to pause rescue efforts, according to state media. Here is what we know so far. What caused the deadly landslide? Initial reports of an earthquake on the Nepal-Tibet border led many to believe that a tremor had caused a landslide, which in turn caused the devastating flood. However, the US Geological Survey has clarified that the disaster was caused by a "glacial collapse", which is when a glacier or part of a glacier disintegrates. The impact of the collapsed glacier hitting the bottom of a valley was so powerful that it registered a magnitude of 5.2, according to USGS data and scientists who have analysed the event. Debris flow from the collapse "caused subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream" the USGS said. Climate change is known to be driving faster glacier melt in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region. Scientists are trying to piece together the exact order of events as rescue efforts continue. Geologist Daniel Shugar – one of the first experts to suggest Wednesday's flash flooding event could have been caused by glacial activity – says glacial thinning inducted by global warming can increase the risk of landslides. But it is still too early to definitively link the event to climate change, Shugar, who is based at the University of Calgary in Canada, tells the BBC. Simon Cook, a geoscientist at the University of Dundee, says however, that climate change "could have an impact". Cook added that his team believed they had identified where the collapse had occured. He told the BBC that the lower part of a glacier in Nepal near the Langtang Lirung peak - approximately 15km (9 miles) west of the site of the floods - had collapsed. He estimated that the glacier collapsed in a north-westerly direction and then travelled westwards downstream. He told the BBC "permafrost is partially holding some mountainsides together, this permafrost is warming and thawing and degrading so you are going to get more landslides". Mike Searle, professor of Earth sciences at Oxford University, said the glacier could have collapsed "hours or days" before the flooding hit Nepal and Tibet. He told the BBC: "I think the sheer wave of debris suggests there was a landslide first, the water built up, (which) dammed the river, and then it burst in one huge great flood." One possibility is that water from rainfall or melting ice may have destabilised the ground or ice, triggering a chain reaction. Scientists will be looking at satellite images of exactly where the landslide occurred, whether any glacial lakes suddenly drained, and where the river might have become blocked, as well as data on recent rainfall. A deluge of material careered towards northern Nepalese towns, including areas popular with mountaineering tourists and pilgrims. The border is around 40 miles (64.4km) north of Nepal's capital city Kathmandu. Footage showed a wall of mud and rock sweeping away buildings, roads and vehicles, as people fled the fast-moving wave of material in the Nuwakot region. In one video, a towering wall of water and mud was seen rushing down a gorge along the Trishuli River and enveloping the Rasuvagadhi Border check point, a multi-storey building. Severe flooding has been reported along the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers. Deaths have also been reported in villages on the Tibetan side of the border. The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIDMOD) has warned secondary flooding could occur in the coming days as a result of the debris that washed into the river systems. The ICIDMOD said they are assessing whether the Trishuli River has been temporarily blocked in narrow sections. If it has been blocked, it is at risk of forming a landslide dam and a second flood. Secondary flood warnings have put people "very much on edge", David Fisher, head of the Red Cross' delegation in Nepal, tells the BBC. How many people are dead and missing? The number of people killed or missing is still becoming clear. Nepali police said at least 475 people had died as of Friday morning local time, with hundreds still missing. Among those killed, 64 were found in downstream areas in the Chitwan district while another 26 were found in Nawalparasi East. Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said 910 people were still missing as of Thursday evening. This included 517 foreign citizens, 44 members of the Nepali army and 28 police officers. The Nepal Tourism Board meanwhile said 644 tourists were still missing, 33 of which were UK nationals, including a 13-year-old girl and 14-year-old boy. It is unclear if any of them are included in the latest death toll. - 'High risk' of lake breaching and causing second flood, warns China - Published38 minutes ago - Collapsed glacier likely caused devastating Nepal-Tibet floods, scientists say - Published5 hours ago Meanwhile, the number of people missing in the mudslide disaster in Tibet's Gyirong county had risen to 558, China's state broadcaster CCTV said on Thursday. Among these are 260 foreign nationals, CCTV said, adding that the death toll remained at three. It is not clear if any of the missing in the Nepali and Chinese figures have been counted twice. China's Premier Li Qiang on Thursday arrived in Gyirong to supervise rescue and relief operations. The border at Gyirong is the main crossing point for tourists and traffic between China and Nepal. How are governments responding? Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said "the entire nation has been left shocked and deeply distressed" and that officials would coordinate with China on the response. China's President Xi Jinping urged an "all-out" search and promised stronger monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary impacts. In neighbouring India, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said his government was "prepared to provide Nepal with all possible types of humanitarian assistance". UN Secretary General António Guterres says he is "saddened by the severe flooding", adding that UN teams and partners are mobilising supplies and personnel in Nepal to support the government-led response. The US has promised $500,000 (£367,982) in aid which will be used to cover emergency shelter, water, sanitation and other relief items for communities affected by the floods. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK has offered £5m to help the Nepalese government and will do "everything we can" to support British nationals in Nepal. Which countries are the missing tourists from? Tourists from all over the world come to Nepal for its mountains and sacred sites. Official figures have suggested at least 291 foreigners are among the missing, including: - India - the Nepal Tourism board says 288 nationals from neighbouring India are missing - China - The Chinese foreign ministry says nearly 100 Chinese nationals are missing in Nepal - US - the latest update from Nepal's tourist board is that 65 US tourists are known to be among the missing - Ukraine - Ukraine's foreign ministry says 53 Ukrainian nationals are missing - Malaysia - 51 Malaysians travelling with Fishtail Tours and Travels are missing in the floods, officials say - Australia - Australia's foreign minister says 39 Australians are among the missing and there's an "unfortunate possibility" the number will rise - UK - Nepal's police say 33 British nationals are missing - Canada - a tourism board spokesman in Nepal says 24 Canadians are reported missing Smaller numbers of travellers from South Korea, South Africa, Portugal, the Netherlands and New Zealand are also among the missing.

item.title: Allan Little: I met dangerously fanatical Mladić early in Bosnian war
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgl744j0ww1o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Allan Little: I met dangerously fanatical Mladić early in Bosnian war - Published Bosnian Serb commander Ratko Mladić, dubbed the "Butcher of Bosnia" for his actions during the Balkan wars of the 1990s, has died in prison. BBC special correspondent Allan Little was there throughout the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, and met Mladić in the early months of the Bosnian war. At night, you could watch the fires of ethnic cleansing across the landscape. The flames provided the only light under the night sky and the black valley would glimmer with flecks of orange. You could watch the men of our village move about silently in the shadows of their homes, each armed with some ancient weapon salvaged from wars long ago and, like the fears and the suspicions and the distrusts, handed down through the generations. One morning I watched a procession of men and women emerge from a forest. They had been driven from their homes two days earlier and had fled with what they could carry. Most were on foot. Some were crammed into the back of ancient farm vehicles drawn by donkeys. There were perhaps 40,000 of them. Their home town had fallen to a Serb advance that had come without warning. Among them, one man seemed close to collapse. He stopped to speak to us. The whole town had fled, he said. He had become separated from his wife in the long trek to safety and was now worried that she had not made it. His pale, almost translucently white skin was stretched across the bones of his face like parchment. His forehead was livid blue from a fall. I asked him how old he was. He said he was 80. "May I ask" I said, "are you a Croat or a Muslim?" The memory of it shames me even now as I hear, in my mind, his answer echo down the years. "I am," he said, "a musician". Our convenient ethnic shorthand reduced them to Serbs, Croats and Muslims. But they were also musicians and scientists and doctors and plumbers and farmers and mothers and fathers and brothers and sisters and very often children. I met Mladić in that first hot summer of the war in Bosnia. We were at Lukavica barracks on the southern edge of Sarajevo. The barracks was awash with weapons and the menacing strut of the paramilitaries. You could buy a Kalashnikov for $200, a hand grenade for just one dollar – the same price, I would soon learn, as the cost of a fresh egg in the besieged city. I shook his hand and he held it fast and pulled me in close. He told me he had just come back from the Sarajevo city centre front line and I saw that he was pumped up by the exhilarating proximity of the fighting. He held my hand for many minutes, fixed me with his eye and told me he was the great defender of brotherhood and unity in former Yugoslavia, and that he dreamed of a world in which there would be no guns and no war. He struck me then as fanatical, dangerously so. In the years that lay ahead, forces under his command committed the worst war crimes on European soil since the Nazis. They bequeathed to the lexicon of war a grim new euphemism - ethnic cleansing. They committed mass murder, extermination, mass rape, forced expulsions. They burned village after village, all in the name of creating an ethnically pure Serbian territory in Croatia and Serbia. Ultimately, at Srebrenica, they committed genocide. Two days after I had met the old musician on that damp muddy roadside, I found myself drawn into the passions of the war in a personal and – at the time – devastating way. My cameraman, Tihomir Tunukovic, a man I had known and worked alongside during the previous 18 months, was killed by a Serb gunner on a ridge above the road he was driving on. We had parted earlier that morning. He was 25 years old, a talented and ambitious young film maker from Zagreb. We drove his body back along the rutted mountain pathways to the coastal city of Split. We broke our hearts at his funeral. The grief of it connected us to the sentiments of the war – the impulse to vengeance and counter vengeance – that were so much a feature of what we were witnessing. General Mladić did not pull the trigger but his command created an atmosphere of wanton permissiveness which cost tens of thousands of lives.
